label: Manners and thanks
rationale: Being polite and grateful: saying thanks, speaking politely, not making a fuss, and the guest's thanks for care and meals.
mixUps: keigo o tsukau (speak politely) and ki o tsukau (fuss over others) share tsukau, and ki o tsukau is not ki o tsukeru (be careful). In osewa ni naru and gochisou ni naru, ni naru puts you on the receiving end; the giver says mendou o miru or ogoru.

targets.trap: English 'thank' leads to kansha suru, which is being grateful (kansha shiteru = I'm grateful), not saying it: 'I have to thank them' is orei iwanakya. orei o suru means giving something back, like a gift or a meal.
partners: oiwai (congratulations: oiwai iitakute = I wanted to congratulate them)
targets.use: For talking about thanking rather than doing it (arigatou does that): orei iwanakya (I have to thank them), chanto orei itta? (did you thank them properly?), orei iitakute (I wanted to say thanks).
targets.notes: orei ni = as thanks: orei ni gohan ogoru yo (dinner's on me, as thanks).

example.ja: 後でちゃんとお礼言わなきゃ。
example.english: I need to thank them properly later.

examplePolite.romaji: ato de chanto orei o iwanakya ikemasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: 後でちゃんとお礼を言わなきゃいけませんね。
examplePolite.english: I really should thank them properly later.

targets.trap: English 'speak keigo' leads to keigo o hanasu, on the model of nihongo o hanasu. It is heard (keigo ga hanasenai), but the everyday verb is tsukau (keigo tsukau), or keigo de hanasu.
partners: kotoba (words: warui kotoba o tsukau = use bad language)
eigo (English: eigo o tsukau shigoto = a job using English)
targets.use: Mostly heard as the offer to drop it: keigo tsukawanakute ii yo (no need to be formal with me), often followed by tameguchi de ii yo (talk to me casually). Also for describing relationships: senpai ni wa keigo tsukau (I speak politely to my seniors).
targets.notes: Sounds like ki tsukawanakute ii yo (don't go to any trouble), the other host line; drill them together.

example.ja: 敬語使わなくていいよ。
example.english: No need to be formal with me.

examplePolite.romaji: keigo wa tsukawanakute ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 敬語は使わなくていいですよ。
examplePolite.english: You don't need to speak formally with me.

targets.verbSense: use, spend; here, spend your attention on others
targets.trap: Not ki o tsukeru (be careful): 'don't go to any trouble' is ki o tsukawanaide, and the mix-up gives ki o tsukenaide, 'don't be careful'.
partners: shinkei (nerves: shinkei tsukau = it takes a lot of care, it's nerve-racking)
targets.use: Hosts and guests say ki o tsukawanakute ii yo or ki o tsukawanaide (don't go to any trouble). About a person, ano hito to iru to ki tsukau means you have to tiptoe around them.
targets.notes: Also written 気を使う; the noun is kizukai (thoughtfulness).

example.ja: そんな気遣わなくていいよ。
example.english: You don't have to fuss over me like that.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna ni ki o tsukawanakute ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: そんなに気を遣わなくていいですよ。
examplePolite.english: Please don't go to any trouble.

targets.verbSense: become; here, come to be in someone's care
targets.trap: English 'thanks for looking after me' leads to sewa shite kurete arigatou, which fits literal care (nursing you when sick, minding your pet). Friends say iroiro arigatou; to hosts, teachers and colleagues the set thanks is osewa ni narimashita.
partners: gochisou (a treat: be treated to a meal)
yakkai (being a burden: rely on someone)
targets.use: Mostly polite and set: kyou kara osewa ni narimasu when you start a stay or a job, osewa ni narimashita (thank you for everything) when you leave a host, job or school. In business you'll hear the humble osewa ni natte orimasu (recognise it, no need to say it). Casual osewa ni natta is used when describing someone who helped you.
targets.notes: gochisou ni naru (be treated to a meal) is built the same way: with ni naru, you are the one receiving. The one doing the looking after says mendou o miru (or sewa o suru).

example.romaji: ano senpai ni wa honto ni osewa ni natta.
example.ja: あの先輩にはほんとにお世話になった。
example.english: That senior really looked out for me.

examplePolite.romaji: ano senpai ni wa hontou ni osewa ni narimashita.
examplePolite.ja: あの先輩には本当にお世話になりました。
examplePolite.english: That senior really looked after me.

targets.verbSense: become; here, come to be the one treated
targets.trap: English 'I got treated' leads to the passive gochisou sareta, which is heard but less usual; people say gochisou ni natta (like osewa ni naru), ogotte moratta or ogorareta. The payer's verbs are ogoru and gochisou suru.
partners: yakkai (imposing: tomodachi no ie ni yakkai ni naru = stay at a friend's place)
targets.use: Said by the one being treated. When someone offers to pay (kyou wa ogoru yo), you accept with jaa, gochisou ni narimasu, and afterwards you thank them with gochisou ni narimashita, to a boss, senpai or host. Among friends gochisousama! does both jobs, and telling someone about it is gochisou ni natta or, more often, ogotte moratta (they paid for me).
targets.notes: gochisou on its own is a feast or treat: sugoi gochisou (what a spread).

example.romaji: kinou senpai ni gochisou ni natta.
example.ja: 昨日先輩にごちそうになった。
example.english: My senpai treated me to a meal yesterday.

examplePolite.ja: 昨日はごちそうになりました。

reviewPool.english: take time off work, miss work
